subject: Chemistry
description: Protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes, atomic number

questions.stem: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is called its:
questions.explanation: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons, identifies the element. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. For a neutral atom, the number of electrons = atomic number. Atomic weight is the weighted average mass of all isotopes. Valency is the combining capacity, usually tied to outer-shell electrons.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called:
questions.explanation: Isotopes — same Z (same element), different A (different neutron count). Example — Carbon-12 and Carbon-14. Isobars — same A but different Z (different elements): argon-40 and calcium-40. Isotones — same number of neutrons but different elements. Isomers — different structural arrangements of the same molecular formula (organic chemistry).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The particle discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897 through cathode-ray experiments was the:
questions.explanation: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays in vacuum tubes. He proposed the 'plum pudding' model of the atom (1904) — electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge. Rutherford discovered the proton (and his 1911 gold-foil experiment gave the nuclear model). Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. The positron (anti-electron) was discovered by Anderson in 1932.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Among the three subatomic particles — electron, proton and neutron — the one with virtually no electrical charge is the:
questions.explanation: Neutron — electrically neutral; mass ~1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Proton — positive charge (+1e); mass ~1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Electron — negative charge (−1e); mass ~9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg (about 1/1,836 of a proton). Mass of an atom is almost entirely in the nucleus (protons + neutrons).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Niels Bohr's atomic model (1913) proposed that electrons move around the nucleus in:

options.option_text: Fixed circular orbits with quantised energies

questions.explanation: Bohr's model (1913) — electrons revolve in specific, quantised circular orbits (shells labelled K, L, M, N, with energies E₁, E₂, E₃, …). An electron emits or absorbs a photon only when jumping between orbits. This successfully explained hydrogen's discrete line spectrum. Modern quantum mechanics replaces the orbit picture with orbital 'clouds' of probability density, but Bohr's quantisation remains a key step.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the L (second) shell of an atom is:
questions.explanation: Capacity of a shell = 2n² where n is the shell number. K (n=1) → 2; L (n=2) → 8; M (n=3) → 18; N (n=4) → 32. The outermost shell — whatever its full capacity — can never hold more than 8 electrons in ground state (the octet rule); Bohr-Bury scheme.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The two stable isotopes of chlorine have mass numbers 35 and 37. Its standard atomic weight (~35.5) reflects:

options.option_text: Weighted average — about 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37

questions.explanation: Chlorine's natural abundance is ~75.8% Cl-35 and ~24.2% Cl-37. Weighted average = 0.758 × 35 + 0.242 × 37 ≈ 35.48. This is why the periodic table lists chlorine's atomic mass as 35.5 rather than a whole number. A simple arithmetic mean of 35 and 37 would give 36 — which is wrong because it ignores abundance.
